summary: Describes DNS over QUIC (DoQ), which carries DNS queries and answers over dedicated QUIC connections for confidentiality. QUIC gives encryption with properties similar to TLS, avoids head-of-line blocking found in TCP, and recovers from packet loss more efficiently. DoQ has privacy properties like DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) with latency closer to plain UDP. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Asking a name-lookup question out loud lets everyone nearby listen in. DNS over QUIC puts the question in a sealed envelope and sends it down a fast private delivery tube.

subtitle: How to carry DNS queries and answers over QUIC, one stream per question, with TLS-style privacy and low latency.

tldr.problem: Plain DNS over UDP is unencrypted, and DNS over TLS runs on TCP, which suffers head-of-line blocking. DNS needed an encrypted transport with latency close to UDP.
tldr.mechanism: DoQ sends each DNS query on its own client-initiated QUIC bidirectional stream, with a 2-octet length prefix, on UDP port 853 with the ALPN token "doq".
tldr.outcome: DoQ gives privacy similar to DNS over TLS and works for stub to recursive, recursive to authoritative and zone transfer traffic. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9250 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2022, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It defines DoQ as a general DNS transport.

sections.title: Goals and Scope of DoQ
sections.content:
RFC 9250 maps the DNS protocol onto the QUIC transport (RFC 9000, RFC 9001) and calls the result DNS over QUIC (DoQ). It has three goals: the same privacy protection as DNS over TLS (RFC 7858), better source address validation for DNS servers than classic DNS over UDP, and a transport that does not impose path MTU limits on the size of DNS responses.

The scope is deliberately wide. DoQ is meant as a general-purpose DNS transport for the stub to recursive resolver case, the recursive resolver to authoritative nameserver case, and nameserver to nameserver traffic such as zone transfers.

The RFC states two non-goals. It makes no attempt to evade blocking of DoQ by middleboxes, and it does not support server-initiated transactions, which are used only in DNS Stateful Operations (RFC 8490).
sections.eli5: DoQ is a way to ask DNS questions privately and quickly. It is meant for phones asking their resolver, resolvers asking name servers, and servers copying zone data to each other.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
This section of the RFC is informative. For privacy, QUIC sets up its security parameters with TLS, so DoQ gives essentially the same protection as DNS over TLS, including the Strict and Opportunistic usage profiles of RFC 8310.

For latency, DoQ uses QUIC's optional 0-RTT data on resumed sessions, long-lived connections that carry many transactions, and one stream per DNS query and response. Separate streams mitigate head-of-line blocking, so a server can answer out of order and a client can use each response as soon as it arrives.

DoQ does not hide itself. The padding it defines obscures which records are in a message, not the fact that the traffic is DNS, so firewalls and other middleboxes might be able to tell DoQ from other QUIC protocols such as HTTP and treat it differently. Only the side that opened the connection may send queries.
sections.eli5: Each question gets its own lane on the road, so a slow answer in one lane never blocks the others. The envelopes are sealed, but anyone can still see they are DNS mail.

sections.title: Connections, Ports and Idle Timeouts
sections.content:
DoQ support is signalled during the QUIC handshake by selecting the ALPN token doq. By default a server MUST listen on UDP port 853, and a client MUST connect to UDP port 853, unless both sides agree on another port. DoQ connections MUST NOT use UDP port 53, to avoid confusion with DNS over UDP. For stub to recursive use, an agreed port 443 can help because it is less likely to be blocked.

Clients and servers SHOULD negotiate an idle timeout, since closing on idle timeout needs no packets. The effective value is the minimum of what the two endpoints advertise. Before sending a new query a client SHOULD check whether the connection has been idle for sufficiently less than the timeout. If so it reuses the connection, and if not it opens a new one. A client with outstanding queries that closes early SHOULD use CONNECTION_CLOSE with DOQ_NO_ERROR.

If a connection fails, all in-progress transactions on it MUST be abandoned. If DoQ cannot be established, clients MAY fall back to DNS over TLS and then possibly cleartext, depending on their usage profile. They SHOULD remember servers that do not support DoQ and not retry for a reasonable period, such as one hour per server.
sections.eli5: A DoQ server waits at a special door, number 853. Once a client is inside, it keeps the door open and reuses it, and closes it quietly if nobody has talked for a while.

sections.title: Stream Mapping and Message IDs
sections.content:
The client picks a separate QUIC stream for each query and the server answers on the same stream. Every DNS message is a 2-octet length field followed by the message as defined in RFC 1035, exactly as in DNS over TCP. So each stream looks like a TCP connection that carries exactly one query.

The client MUST use the next available client-initiated bidirectional stream for each query and MUST signal with STREAM FIN that it will send nothing more. The server MUST send its response or responses on that stream and finish with STREAM FIN. The first query therefore uses stream 0, the second stream 4, and so on. Zone transfers can produce several responses on one stream, which is why the length prefix is needed.

The DNS Message ID MUST be set to 0 in queries, because the stream already pairs queries and responses. When a proxy forwards a DoQ message to another transport it MUST generate an ID by that transport's rules, and when it forwards another transport's message over DoQ it MUST set the ID to 0. Messages are limited to 65535 bytes, and the EDNS(0) UDP size parameter is ignored.
sections.eli5: Every question is written on its own sheet of paper and sent down its own pipe. Because each pipe carries just one question, nobody needs to number the questions.

sections.title: Error Codes and Cancellation
sections.content:
DoQ defines application error codes used to reset streams or close connections. A client cancels a transaction by sending QUIC STOP_SENDING, preferably with DOQ_REQUEST_CANCELLED, and the server SHOULD stop processing. This lets a secondary cancel one zone transfer without closing the connection. A server that cannot answer because of an internal error SHOULD send RESET_STREAM with DOQ_INTERNAL_ERROR. A DNS error such as SERVFAIL is not a transport error and is returned as a normal response.

Protocol violations are fatal. Examples include a non-zero Message ID, a STREAM FIN before the full message arrives, more than one query on a stream, the edns-tcp-keepalive option, or any unidirectional stream. The peer SHOULD close the connection with DOQ_PROTOCOL_ERROR, or MAY silently abandon it. An unknown error code, or one used in an unexpected context, is treated as DOQ_UNSPECIFIED_ERROR.
sections.eli5: If you change your mind about a question, you can say stop for just that one question. If someone breaks the rules, the whole conversation ends.

sections.title: Resumption, 0-RTT, Padding and Zone Transfers
sections.content:
Clients MAY use session resumption and 0-RTT. Only replayable transactions, meaning OPCODE QUERY or NOTIFY, may go in 0-RTT data. A server that gets anything else in 0-RTT MUST queue it until the handshake completes, reply REFUSED with the Extended DNS Error "Too Early", or close with DOQ_PROTOCOL_ERROR. Clients SHOULD use a resumption ticket only once, and by default not resume if their connectivity changed. Servers SHOULD issue tickets with a long lifetime (for example 6 hours).

Implementations MUST pad to protect against traffic analysis, either with the EDNS(0) Padding option or by padding QUIC packets, aligning to a small set of fixed sizes. For address validation they MUST follow RFC 9000, which limits amplification to a factor 3, and SHOULD consider Retry packets.

For zone transfers, servers MUST handle multiple concurrent IXFR and AXFR requests on one connection. Clients SHOULD reuse one connection to the same primary and send requests without waiting for earlier replies. Clients SHOULD send queries concurrently and not wait for an earlier reply, and servers SHOULD answer on each stream as soon as the response is ready.
sections.eli5: Speaking before the secure handshake finishes is only allowed for harmless questions that are fine to hear twice. Messages are padded to a few standard sizes so eavesdroppers cannot guess the contents from the size.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of DoQ should be comparable to those of DNS over TLS (RFC 7858). DoQ relies on QUIC, which relies on TLS 1.3, so it supports the protections against downgrade attacks described in BCP 195. For stub resolvers, DoQ clients SHOULD use a Strict usage profile. Authentication for recursive to authoritative traffic was unspecified at the time of writing.

The privacy section covers several risks. 0-RTT data can be replayed by adversaries, which may let them learn what name was queried by watching the resolver's outgoing traffic. Reusing a resumption ticket or an address validation token can make a client linkable across sessions or locations, and long duration sessions or connection migration have a similar effect. By default clients SHOULD prioritize privacy and start new sessions if their connectivity changes. Packet lengths and timing can also reveal which site is being loaded, which padding is meant to mitigate.
sections.eli5: A sealed envelope still has a size and a delivery time, and using the same stamp twice lets a watcher link your letters. DoQ advises padding, stamps used once, and starting fresh when you move.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the ALPN identification string doq (bytes 0x64 0x6F 0x71). It also updated the existing port 853 entry (service name domain-s) to cover UDP, with the description "DNS query-response protocol run over DTLS or QUIC". QUIC version 1 can coexist with DTLS on that port.

It registered Extended DNS Error code 26, "Too Early", and created a new "DNS-over-QUIC Error Codes" registry governing a 62-bit space. Values 0x00 to 0x3f are assigned by Standards Action or IESG Approval, and larger permanent values use Specification Required.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official phone book of the Internet. DoQ got its own name tag, "doq", and shares door number 853 with the older DNS-over-TLS service.
